steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on getting reliable predictive uncertainty from deep neural networks. Explain why current Bayesian deep learning methods fall short, introduce our density uncertainty criterion and density uncertainty layers, summarize the experiments, and list the contributions.

steps.text:
- Why predictive uncertainty matters; neural nets are overconfident
- Bayesian deep learning and where VI falls short
- Density uncertainty criterion
- Density uncertainty layer
- Experiments
- Contributions

  - paper: reliable predictive uncertainty with deep NNs
- Problem with existing approaches
  - Bayesian deep learning: principled, uncertainty about parameters (cite)

  - Figure 1 a-c: collapsed or flat uncertainty around origin, though no training data there
- Density uncertainty criterion
  - new criterion + new stochastic NN architecture
  - predictive uncertainty grounded in empirical density of input: higher for improbable inputs, lower for probable
  - motivation: Bayesian linear regression adheres to it
- Density uncertainty layer
  - stochastic architecture designed to satisfy criterion
  - fit energy-based model of input; constraint on predictive variance from approximate posterior
  - flexible building block for density-aware deep NNs
  - Figure 1 d: high uncertainty in low-density region around origin

  - compare with popular uncertainty methods (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models have been successful in many applications, and this has caused a lot of interest in deploying them for real-world predictions. But in high-stakes domains, like healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, the model's prediction is crucial and so is its predictive uncertainty. One challenge is that conventional neural networks do not have a robust mechanism to quantify uncertainty, and they tend to make overconfident predictions. This paper is about how to get reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty with deep neural networks.

Why is this a problem? Bayesian deep learning gives a principled framework to quantify predictive uncertainty, by including uncertainty about the model parameters. But the common variational inference (VI) approaches that approximate the parameter posterior in Bayesian deep learning often do not provide reliable predictive uncertainty. For example, Figure 1 a-c shows that these methods give either collapsed or flat predictive uncertainty around the origin, even if no training data was observed in that region.

In this work we propose a new criterion for reliable predictive uncertainty and a new stochastic neural network architecture that satisfies the criterion. The density uncertainty criterion says that the predictive uncertainty of a model should be grounded in the empirical density of the input. So we should see higher uncertainty for improbable inputs and lower uncertainty for more probable inputs. As a motivation, we will show that Bayesian linear regression already adheres to the criterion.

- Density uncertainty layer
  - stochastic architecture designed to satisfy the criterion
  - fit energy-based model of input; constrain predictive variance of approximate posterior
  - flexible building block for density-aware deep NNs
  - Figure 1 d: high uncertainty in low-density region around origin
- Experiments
  - UCI and CIFAR-10/100 uncertainty benchmarks; compare to popular uncertainty methods
  - more reliable uncertainty estimates, robust OOD detection
- Contributions
  - 1. criterion (training density of input)
  - 2. layer, general building block
  - 3. UCI + CIFAR-10/100 study, better than existing approaches on both

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models have been successful in many applications, and this has caused a lot of interest in deploying them for real-world predictions. But in high-stakes domains, like healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, the model's prediction is crucial and so is its predictive uncertainty. One challenge is that conventional neural networks do not have a robust mechanism to quantify uncertainty, and they tend to make overconfident predictions. This paper is about how to get reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty with deep neural networks.

Why is this a problem? Bayesian deep learning gives a principled framework to quantify predictive uncertainty, by including uncertainty about the model parameters. But the common variational inference (VI) approaches that approximate the parameter posterior in Bayesian deep learning often do not provide reliable predictive uncertainty. For example, Figure 1 a-c shows that these methods give either collapsed or flat predictive uncertainty around the origin, even if no training data was observed in that region.

In this work we propose a new criterion for reliable predictive uncertainty and a new stochastic neural network architecture that satisfies the criterion. The density uncertainty criterion says that the predictive uncertainty of a model should be grounded in the empirical density of the input. So we should see higher uncertainty for improbable inputs and lower uncertainty for more probable inputs. As a motivation, we will show that Bayesian linear regression already adheres to the criterion.

Then we develop the density uncertainty layer, which is a stochastic neural network architecture designed to satisfy the density uncertainty criterion. The idea is to fit an energy-based model of the input, and then satisfy the density uncertainty criterion with a constraint on the predictive variance that the approximate posterior produces. Density uncertainty layers are a flexible building block for density-aware deep neural networks. Figure 1 d shows how Density Uncertainty gives high predictive uncertainty in the low-density region around the origin in the input space.

We study density uncertainty layers on the UCI and CIFAR-10/100 uncertainty benchmarks, and we compare the proposed method to popular uncertainty estimation methods for neural networks. We find that the proposed density-aware neural networks give more reliable predictive uncertainty estimates and robust out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions.

1. We propose the density uncertainty criterion for reliable predictive uncertainty, which says that the predictive uncertainty of a model should be grounded in the training density of the input.

2. We present the density uncertainty layer. Its predictive uncertainty adheres to the density uncertainty criterion, and it is a general building block for uncertainty-aware neural networks.

3. We study the density uncertainty layers on the UCI and CIFAR-10/100 uncertainty estimation benchmarks. The method performs better than existing approaches on both benchmarks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The success of deep learning models in a range of applications has spurred significant interest in deploying them for real-world predictions. But in high-stakes domains, such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, both the model's prediction and its predictive uncertainty are crucial. A challenge is that conventional neural networks lack a robust mechanism for quantifying uncertainty, and they tend to produce overconfident predictions [1,2]. This paper is about how to produce reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty with deep neural networks.

Why is this a problem? Bayesian deep learning offers a principled framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty by incorporating uncertainty about the model parameters [3,4,5,6]. However, the common variational inference (VI) approaches used to approximate the parameter posterior in Bayesian deep learning [3,6,7,8] often fail to provide reliable predictive uncertainty [9,10]. For example, Figure 1 a-c demonstrate that these methods produce either collapsed or flat predictive uncertainty around the origin, even though no training data were observed there.

In this work, we propose a novel criterion for reliable predictive uncertainty and a new stochastic neural network architecture that satisfies it. The density uncertainty criterion posits that a model's predictive uncertainty should be grounded in the empirical density of the input. That is, we should see higher uncertainty for improbable inputs and lower uncertainty for more probable ones. As motivation, we will show that Bayesian linear regression inherently adheres to the criterion.

We then develop the density uncertainty layer, a stochastic neural network architecture designed to satisfy the density uncertainty criterion. The idea is to fit an energy-based model of the input and then satisfy the density uncertainty criterion via a constraint on the predictive variance produced by the approximate posterior. Density uncertainty layers serve as a flexible building block for density-aware deep neural networks. Figure 1 d shows how Density Uncertainty produces high predictive uncertainty in the low-density region of the input space around the origin.

We study density uncertainty layers on the UCI and CIFAR-10/100 uncertainty benchmarks, comparing the proposed method to popular uncertainty estimation methods for neural networks [6,7,11,8]. We find that the proposed density-aware neural networks provide more reliable predictive uncertainty estimates and robust out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance.

Contributions. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions.

- 1. We propose the density uncertainty criterion for reliable predictive uncertainty, which asserts that a model's predictive uncertainty should be grounded in the training density of the input.

- 2. We present the density uncertainty layer, whose predictive uncertainty adheres to the density uncertainty criterion and which serves as a general building block for uncertainty-aware neural networks.

- 3. We study the proposed density uncertainty layers on the UCI and CIFAR-10/100 uncertainty estimation benchmarks. On both benchmarks, the method performs better than existing approaches.
